body_text: MyMD Pharmaceuticals® Advances Phase 2 Multi-Center Clinical Trial of MYMD-1® as a Therapy for Delaying Aging and Extending Healthy Lifespan July 26, 2022 7:30am EDT Download as PDF Sarcopenia trial shows no evidence of toxicity or safety issues and patients were enrolled in the next higher dose of MYMD-1 BALTIMORE--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- MyMD Pharmaceuticals, Inc. ® (Nasdaq: MYMD) (“MyMD” or “the Company”), a clinical stage pharmaceutical company committed to developing novel therapies for age-related diseases, autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, announced further advancement of its fully funded Phase 2 clinical trial of lead drug candidate MYMD-1 ® as a therapy for delaying aging and expanding healthy lifespan. To date, the trial has completed dosing for the first patient cohort and dosing has been initiated in the next higher dose cohort. The trial’s Safety Review Committee has confirmed no safety issues and no toxicity in the prior cohort and has voted unanimously to escalate to the next higher dose and begin enrolling the next cohort. The Phase 2 multi-center double-blind, placebo controlled, randomized study ( NCT05283486 ) investigates the efficacy, tolerability and pharmacokinetics of MYMD-1 in the treatment of chronic inflammation associated with sarcopenia/frailty in participants aged 65 years or older. “As agreed upon with the FDA, the primary endpoint of our Phase 2 multi-center study is to demonstrate reduced levels of TNF-alpha (TNF-α), a key player in associated pathological aging, in the blood of patients,” said Chris Chapman, MD, President, Director and Chief Medical Officer of MyMD. “Having already demonstrated the drug’s mechanism of action and efficacy in Phase 1, achieving the same primary endpoint as our current trial, we are pleased with the progress in Phase 2 to date. We continue to advance the trial and expect efficacy data in the second half of 2022.” In the Phase 1 dose-ranging study of MYMD-1 for delaying aging, subjects were treated with MYMD-1 or placebo and TNF-α levels were measured pre- and post-treatment. The data demonstrated a statistically significant decrease in TNF-alpha levels (p-value <0.05) found in MYMD-1 treated subjects, but no change in the participants given placebo. This data was consistent with outcomes from pre-clinical models pointing to the drug’s potential role in reducing both frailty and inflammatory cytokines. Market Opportunity MyMD has not identified any other FDA-approved drugs for treating aging disorders and extending healthy lifespan humans, a market expected to be at least $600 billion by 20251 according to a major investment bank. TNF-α blockers are the most prescribed drugs by revenue, a global market of approximately $40 billion per year.2 Aging is closely linked to multi-morbidities, frailty, and death due to conditions such as neoplastic, cardiovascular, neurodegenerative, metabolic, or autoimmune diseases.3 Similarly, frailty, or a decline in physical function leading to greater risk of hospitalization, disability, and death, increases with age independent of underlying conditions or demographical characteristics.4 About MYMD-1 MYMD-1, an oral selective inhibitor of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), a driver of chronic inflammation, is being studied to slow the aging process, prevent sarcopenia and frailty, and extend healthy lifespan. MYMD-1 has shown effectiveness in pre-clinical and clinical studies in regulating the immune system. Unlike other therapies, MYMD-1 has been shown in these studies to selectively block TNF-α when it becomes overactivated in autoimmune diseases and cytokine storms, but not block it from doing its normal job of being a first responder to any routine type of moderate infection. MYMD-1’s ease of oral dosing is another differentiator compared to currently available TNF-α blockers, all of which require delivery by injection or infusion. No FDA-approved TNF inhibitor has ever been dosed orally. In addition, the drug is not immunosuppressive and has not been shown to cause the serious side effects common with traditional therapies that treat inflammation. Because it can cross the blood-brain barrier and gain access to the central nervous system (CNS), MYMD-1 is also positioned to be a possible treatment for brain-related disorders. Its mechanism of action and efficacy in diseases including multiple sclerosis (MS) and thyroiditis have been studied through collaborations with several academic institutions. About MyMD Pharmaceuticals, Inc. MyMD Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Nasdaq: MYMD), a clinical stage pharmaceutical company committed to developing novel therapies for autoimmune and inflammatory conditions, is focused on developing two novel therapeutic platforms that treat the causes of disease rather than only addressing the symptoms. MYMD-1 is a drug platform based on a clinical stage small molecule that regulates the immune system to control TNF-α, which drives chronic inflammation, and other pro-inflammatory cell signaling cytokines. MYMD-1 is being developed to delay aging, increase longevity, and treat autoimmune diseases. The Company’s second drug platform, Supera-CBD , is being developed to treat chronic pain, addiction and epilepsy. Supera-CBD is a novel synthetic derivative of cannabidiol (CBD) and is being developed to address and improve upon the rapidly growing CBD market, which includes both FDA approved drugs and CBD products not currently regulated as drugs. title: ABS vs. PETG: Differences and Comparison
summary: Comparing ABS vs. PETG enables manufacturers to decide which material is best suited for their application.
body_text: ABS vs. PETG: Applications Comparison ABS vs. PETG for application comparison highlights the distinct advantages of each material based on their properties. ABS is used in automotive parts, toys, and household appliances due to its strength, impact resistance, and higher heat tolerance. PETG is preferred in medical devices, can be used in food-safe applications if certified, but most 3D printing PETG is not food safe, and structural parts require clarity, flexibility, and good chemical resistance. ABS is more suited for applications demanding durability under stress and higher operating temperatures. PETG excels in environments where moisture or chemical exposure is prevalent and offers better resistance to sunlight (UV) than ABS. The differences inform material selection for specific use cases based on performance requirements. ABS vs. PETG: Part Accuracy Comparison ABS vs. PETG for part accuracy reveals clear differences in dimensional accuracy and layer adhesion. ABS tends to shrink as it cools after printing, which can lead to warping and changes in part dimensions, making it more difficult to meet stringent tolerance requirements. PETG exhibits better layer adhesion and less shrinkage during cooling, resulting in parts that maintain dimensions more consistently. The reduced warping of PETG contributes to higher dimensional stability and better overall part accuracy for larger prints or designs with tight specifications. PETG is a more reliable choice when high precision and consistency are critical because of its characteristics. ABS vs. PETG: Speed Comparison ABS vs. PETG for speed comparison highlights the differences in printing efficiency. ABS and PETG typically print in the 40–60 mm/s range for best results. High-end machines may push PETG faster, but it's not standard. ABS requires higher printing temperatures, around 230 °C to 250 °C, and a heated print bed to prevent warping, which can slow setups. PETG uses elevated extrusion temperatures (around 220 °C to 260 °C) and a heated bed, but its lower susceptibility to warping and better layer adhesion contribute to fewer print failures and more efficient print cycles. ABS vs. PETG: Surface Comparison ABS vs. PETG for surface comparison highlights the differences in finish and smoothness. ABS can produce a reasonably smooth surface when printed correctly, but it is more prone to warping and layer delamination than PETG, which can lead to visible surface imperfections on larger parts. PETG offers better layer adhesion and reduced warping, resulting in more consistent surface quality and fewer visible lines. PETG’s natural clarity and smooth finish make it suitable for parts where a polished or semi‑transparent appearance is desired. PETG requires less surface refinement to achieve a visually appealing part, while ABS surface quality can be improved through post‑processing (such as acetone smoothing). ABS vs. PETG: Heat Resistance ABS vs. PETG for heat resistance reveals key differences in performance under elevated temperatures. ABS has a glass transition temperature of ~105 °C, but mechanical strength begins to degrade below this point, especially under load. PETG typically begins to soften around 75–85 °C, with deformation occurring earlier under mechanical stress. ABS’s higher working temperature tolerance makes it a more appropriate choice for parts subjected to sustained heat. PETG’s lower heat resistance makes it more suitable for applications that do not experience prolonged high temperatures, while offering good performance in moderate thermal environments. ABS vs. PETG: Biodegradability Comparison ABS vs. PETG for biodegradability comparison shows clear differences in environmental impact. ABS and PETG are non‑biodegradable thermoplastics that persist in the environment under natural conditions and do not break down easily. The two materials are recyclable, though PETG is easier to recycle in practice. The recyclability of PETG helps reduce its environmental footprint when processed by appropriate recycling systems, while ABS recycling may require more specialized facilities. Neither ABS nor PETG is biodegradable; both are non‑biodegradable petroleum‑based thermoplastics, but PETG has a stronger recycling pathway, which is preferable for end-of-life handling. ABS vs. PETG: Toxicity Comparison ABS vs. PETG for toxicity comparison reveals differences in material safety during production and use. ABS releases strong, potentially toxic fumes when heated during 3D printing, making good ventilation or air filtration systems essential for safe operation. PETG produces fumes that are not as strong or hazardous as ABS’s emissions, though exposure to volatile organic compounds (VOCs) must be minimized in any printing environment. Printing it in enclosed spaces or home settings presents lower risks compared to ABS, which is considered more problematic without adequate ventilation because PETG’s emissions are less intense. PETG’s lower emission profile makes it a safer choice for indoor applications where exposure to fumes must be reduced. ABS vs. PETG: Cost Comparison ABS vs. PETG for cost comparison shows clear differences in material pricing and printing expenses. ABS filament is generally less expensive than PETG filament, making it a more economical choice when material cost is a priority, particularly for larger runs or volume printing. Lower ABS material cost reduces upfront expenses, especially for parts that require strength and higher temperature performance without premium pricing. PETG filament is typically priced higher, reflecting its broader versatility, chemical resistance, and easier printing characteristics. PETG’s printing ease and lower risk of failures can reduce indirect costs related to setup and reprints, even if its raw material cost per part is higher. ABS provides cost advantages where budget constraints and mechanical performance are key factors, while PETG’s higher price corresponds with its balanced performance features. Is PETG Stronger Than ABS? No, PETG has higher impact resistance than ABS in many cases, but ABS is stronger under compression and heat. ABS is more rigid and durable under stress, making it better suited for high-stress applications, while PETG offers good strength and flexibility. PETG is typically more impact-resistant and ductile; ABS can crack under impact, making it ideal for automotive parts and heavy-duty functional components. PETG is more flexible and less prone to breaking under tension, but its strength under compression or impact does not match that of ABS. The difference in mechanical properties makes ABS the better choice for high-stress applications, while PETG is preferred in areas requiring flexibility and chemical resistance. Is PETG Heat Resistant Compared to ABS? No, PETG is not as heat-resistant as ABS. PETG handles temperatures up to 70-80°C before it begins to soften or deform, making it more suitable for moderate heat environments, while ABS maintains its structural integrity up to around 100°C. The difference in heat tolerance makes ABS the better choice for parts exposed to elevated temperatures (automotive components or electrical housings). PETG is more suitable for applications where moderate heat resistance is sufficient, such as in food packaging or consumer products. Is PETG UV Resistant? No, PETG is not highly UV resistant. PETG is prone to degradation over time when exposed to prolonged sunlight, while it offers better UV stability than many other plastics. PETG can lose its strength, color, and clarity when exposed to ultraviolet rays, making it less suitable for outdoor applications without additional protective coatings. Materials like ABS, though not UV-resistant in the strictest sense, ABS performs worse than PETG in UV exposure unless specially treated. PETG is better suited for indoor applications or environments with minimal UV exposure. PETG can be treated with UV stabilizers or coatings for improved UV resistance in outdoor applications. What is the PETG vs ABS for Outdoor Use PETG vs ABS for outdoor use shows clear differences in UV resistance and weathering. PETG generally has better UV resistance than ABS, though neither is truly UV‑resistant without additives, making it more vulnerable to degradation when exposed to prolonged sunlight. PETG’s UV stability is limited, causing it to degrade over time, resulting in fading, brittleness, and loss of strength, while the two materials offer some resistance to weathering. ABS performs poorly outdoors unless UV‑stabilized; ASA is the ABS‑derived material designed for outdoor UV exposure. ABS is rarely used unmodified for outdoor exposure; it requires coatings, stabilizers, or replacement with ASA. PETG is better suited for indoor use or applications with minimal UV exposure unless treated with a protective coating. What are the Mutual Alternatives to ABS and PETG? The mutual alternatives to ABS and PETG are listed below. Nylon : Nylon is a versatile thermoplastic material known for its excellent impact resistance, flexibility, and durability, which makes it comparable to ABS and PETG in many applications, but with superior abrasion resistance. Nylon performs well in FDM 3D printing for parts that require strength and wear resistance. The material is highly resistant to abrasion and has good chemical resistance, making it suitable for functional parts such as gears, bearings, and automotive components. Polycarbonate : Polycarbonate is another alternative with outstanding impact resistance and strength. Polycarbonate offers better heat resistance than ABS and PETG, making it ideal for high-performance applications. The material is used in applications that require transparency, high strength, and toughness (protective covers, optical lenses, and electrical housings). What are the Similarities Between ABS and PETG? The similarities between ABS and PETG are listed below. Non-Biodegradable : ABS and PETG are non-biodegradable, meaning the materials do not naturally break down in the environment and can contribute to long-term pollution if not correctly disposed of. Susceptibility to Moisture : ABS and PETG are susceptible to moisture absorption, which can affect their printing properties, though PETG has better moisture resistance compared to ABS. ABS and PETG need to be kept dry during storage to prevent issues such as bubbling or weak layers. High-Temperature Printing : ABS and PETG are used in 3D printing processes that require high extrusion temperatures. The materials are compatible with printers that operate at elevated temperatures, ranging from 220°C to 250°C, to ensure proper melting and layer bonding. Recyclability : ABS and PETG are recyclable, which allows them to be reprocessed and reused in the production of new products. Recycling the materials reduces waste and their environmental impact when handled properly through recycling systems. What are Other Comparisons for ABS Besides PETG? The other comparison for ABS, besides PETG, is listed below. ABS vs. PLA : PLA (polylactic acid) is a biodegradable plastic that is more rigid than ABS, though it is weaker and more brittle. PLA is easier to print and is well-suited for hobbyist projects due to its lower heat resistance, while ABS has better durability and impact resistance. High-temperature applications make PLA unsuitable for parts that are exposed to heat. Toughness is not due to weight difference; it's due to material ductility and impact resistance. ABS vs. ASA : ASA (Acrylonitrile styrene-acrylate) is a high-performance plastic similar to ABS, used in applications requiring high strength. ASA has superior UV resistance, making it better for outdoor use compared to ABS, which degrades under sunlight exposure. The cost of ASA is higher than that of ABS, but it is durable, impact-resistant, and weather-resistant, making it ideal for applications in outdoor environments ( automotive and outdoor signage). What are Other Comparisons for PETG Besides ABS? The other comparisons for PETG besides ABS are listed below. PETG vs. PET : PETG is derived from PET by replacing the glycol molecule with a larger monomer, resulting in better shock resistance and higher temperature tolerance. PETG provides improved impact resistance and flexibility, making it more suitable for applications requiring toughness and flexibility, while PET has similar or slightly better heat resistance but is more prone to crystallization, making it harder to print. PETG vs. TPU : PETG is tougher but less flexible than TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane). TPU is more flexible and suitable for applications that require elasticity, such as phone cases or wearable parts. A more rigid PETG is better suited to applications requiring strength and clarity. PETG needs a heated bed temperature between 60°C and 80°C, while TPU typically prints at 210–240 °C; 40–60 °C refers to the heated bed, not the nozzle, making TPU easier to print in some cases.
